article.title: ETH Zurich Simulations Show Venus Rift Valleys Widening Up to 10 Centimeters a Year, Pointing to Active Tectonics
article.summary: New 3D simulations and Nature Geoscience findings suggest Venus's rift valleys are geologically young or still moving, challenging the view of a dormant planet.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Venus's vast rift valleys may be far younger, and far more active, than scientists have long assumed. A team at ETH Zurich built high-resolution 3D computer simulations of Venusian rifting and found that rifts widen at a rate of [3 to 10 centimeters per year](https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2026/07/venus-dead-far-from-it.html), a pace fast enough to mark them as either currently active or only recently stopped. The study was published in [Nature Geoscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-026-02044-8) on July 24, 2026.

## What We Know

Venus's rift valleys, canyon-like features carved by tectonic stretching, can [span up to 10,000 kilometers](https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2026/07/venus-dead-far-from-it.html) across the planet's surface. Scientists have generally believed these features [originated more than 100 million years ago](https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2026/07/venus-dead-far-from-it.html) and were left over from a more tectonically active past.

The new research, led by Xi Yang — [a master's student working under the supervision of Taras Gerya](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-young-rift-flanks-venus-tectonically.html), professor of geodynamics at ETH Zurich's Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences — used the first high-resolution three-dimensional simulations of Venusian rift structures, moving beyond earlier two-dimensional models, according to [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-young-rift-flanks-venus-tectonically.html). The team's models show that [broad ridges, known as rift flanks, form along the edges of rift valleys when the rifts are geologically young and either still actively moving or have only recently stopped moving](https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2026/07/venus-dead-far-from-it.html). Once tectonic movement ceases, those flanks flatten out over time.

Critically, the simulated wide, elevated flanks were not just a model artifact. [Wide and high rift flanks are not only produced by the computer model but can also be seen in images of the Venusian surface from the Magellan probe during its 1990s mission](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-young-rift-flanks-venus-tectonically.html), giving the team an observational check against real Venusian terrain. One of the rift systems the team compared its models against is Dali Chasma, where the ETH release presents a side-by-side comparison of a simulated crustal model against the actual rift system on Venus.

The [Nature Geoscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-026-02044-8) paper, co-authored by Yang, Gerya, and Anna J. P. Gülcher, states that the team's 3D thermomechanical experiments were designed "to systematically investigate the rifting dynamics and topography under Venusian conditions," and that the results "demonstrate that wide rift flank uplifts strongly indicate either presently ongoing Venusian rifting or activity within the past few tens of millions of years."

Gerya said the findings sharpen scientists' picture of the planet's inner workings. "The results help us to better assess the tectonic activity on Venus," [he said](https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2026/07/venus-dead-far-from-it.html). Taken together with the modeling results, [the researchers conclude that Venus remains an active planet with a more dynamic interior than previously believed](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-young-rift-flanks-venus-tectonically.html).

## What We Don't Know

The study identifies rift flank width as a signature of recent or ongoing activity, but it cannot yet pin down exactly which of Venus's many rift systems are moving right now versus which stopped moving some tens of millions of years ago — a distinction the researchers describe in terms of a broad window rather than a precise date. The findings also rely on comparing simulated topography to decades-old Magellan radar imagery, since no orbiter has mapped Venus's surface at higher resolution since the 1990s.

That gap is expected to close in the next decade. [ETH geophysics professors Paul Tackley and Gerya, along with their collaborators, are participating in ESA's EnVision mission](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-young-rift-flanks-venus-tectonically.html), which is [scheduled for launch in the early 2030s](https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2026/07/venus-dead-far-from-it.html) and will study the planet more thoroughly, from its core to its upper atmosphere. Tackley and Gerya are developing orbiter instruments for that mission, according to the [ETH Zurich release](https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2026/07/venus-dead-far-from-it.html).

## Why It Matters

Venus and Earth are similar in size and bulk composition, but Venus lacks Earth-style plate tectonics, and researchers have debated for decades how much internal geological activity the planet still has. Evidence that at least some of its rift systems are geologically young or actively moving would suggest Venus's interior is still releasing heat through localized tectonic stretching, rather than being effectively frozen in place. Confirming or refining that picture is one of the scientific goals EnVision is designed to help address once it reaches Venus orbit in the next decade.
